You cannot claim that any insecticide is environmentally safe - never mind targets just one species! - when there is a large, irrefutable body of evidence that insect, butterfly, bee, avian and amphibian populations are all plummeting and we humans are to blame.

A single opossum will devour thousands of ticks, other wild mammals too, yet people keep killing them. If deer numbers are increasing, it’s because climate change is making more food available in more places for longer periods during the year. Natural predators are increasingly scarce. Deer go through cycles where populations grow beyond the ability of the local environment to support them, then they starve and populations drop, until the cycle begins anew. This has always been the case, and it’s worse now because of us. 

Yet the author advocates pouring more chemicals into this catastrophic mess… Is it not yet clear that when humans try to “manage” nature and “fix” problems they created, they just end up making a bigger mess?

I remember hearing about alpha-gal about 15 years ago. As I recall author John Grisham was interviewed about having it. And a UVA doctor figured it out. I thought at the time, add it to the list of tick bite consequences which the CDC and IDSA will try to downplay.  

I’m very sorry to see the explosion in cases and hope this will result in better outcomes due to stories like this. 
Twenty+ years ago our family members incurred tick bites around the same time (due to no awareness of the threat in our heavily wooded backyard). Subsequent positive blood tests (undertaken by Lyme-literate doctors) included Borrelia burgdorferi, babesia microti, babesia WA-1, ehrlichia, Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever, and bartonella henselae, and, highly elevated Epstein Barr and mycoplasma pneumonia levels. Consequences included PANDAS (autoimmune encephalitis) in our 5 year old, two simultaneous thyroid diseases (Hashimotos and Graves) in one adult, neurological deficits including tremors, sensitivity to light, and sudden onset short term memory loss. 

What is still desperately needed is for the more medical professionals to be trained to recognize how many illnesses can result from tick bites, and how to treat them.

https://www.ilads.org/research-literature/lyme-disease-basics-for-providers/
https://www.lymedisease.org/coinfections-lyme-times/

During the Bush administration, Scooter Libby was prosecuted for leaking classified information to Judith Miller, a Times reporter. Ms. Miller was subpoenaed to testify before a grand jury. She refused to testify and was held in contempt and imprisoned. 

During Obama’s presidency, leaks of classified information were pursued more aggressively than before, and a number of reporters were subpoenaed. 

Before Trump, the Justice Department required high level approval for reporter subpoenas. There was a brief section in the US Attorney’s Manual that spelled out the policy. Journalists had long sought a privilege that would restrict subpoenas aggressively. No such privilege exists but it was widely understood that journalists merited special protection. 

Shortly after Trump took office, a long, detailed section was added to the US Attorney’s Manual, filled with legalese, purportedly designed to spell the whole thing out.  Clearly, Trump was abandoning what you might call a gentleman’s agreement, replacing it with what you might call a tirade that foretold of more aggressive enforcement and a hypertechnical approach. Most important the new language made it clear that Trump had little trust in reporters and so he was going to spell the whole thing out, backing far away from any notion that there could an informal understanding bordering on privilege.

Ask it to write something new that it can't copy from somewhere else and it's obvious that it doesn't know what it's talking about. I've read too many poorly written documents written by AI that might fool someone who doesn't know the subject.

On top of the LLM, you have psychological tricks and human reinforcement to make it sound more authoritative or agreeable depending on the model. They've added tons of special cases for solving certain classes of problems that require some computation. For cybersecurity, it's mostly a matter of throwing more compute at the problem with techniques that have been known for decades. I am a computer scientist.

It's not artificial superintelligence and LLMs can't achieve that.

Use a credit card that doesn't charge "foreign fees" and same for ATMs to get local currencyDon't eat in fast food chains - why travel to europe? use google, tripadvisor to eat locally from the locals . eat where locals are gathered.lean into airb&b - read reviews, take what brits have to say closer to what you will like . If you go for a hotel- pick small, local boutiques with good reviews don't try to go everyhwere. Pick a place for 2-3 days of exploration. So one week calls for 2 places max. 2 weeks - 4. Melatonin is your friend for first 2-3 days, avoid alcohol for first couple of days, hydrate . Do NOT go to bed on your frist day there until evenig.

comments.name: F Busoni
comments.body:
Exemplification of an oxymoron:

“European vacation.”

comments.name: Leighton Schmitt
comments.body: We have embraced travelling to the South of Europe in Jan/Feb, and the north of Europe in April and May. We were never beach people, so for easy, crowd free access to the top sights, cheaper rooms, and no sweating through our shirts, we love winter and spring.

comments.name: Rip
comments.body: If only the “paradox of choice” applied to reading, not just watching, and to books, not just movies. But the watching movies has completely displaced the reading books in our screen and devices culture, for children as well as adults.

comments.name: Susan F
comments.body: Fascinating article! But two-year-olds shouldn't be watching movies! They should be looking at books, puzzles, Nature! They should be having tactile experiences.  It's so much easier to plant them in front of the TV--I get that--but it's not great for their development. Maybe another article about keeping screens away from little ones is in order.

comments.name: Susan Sosna
comments.body: Likewise for listening to music.  There is research showing the same paradox of balancing the predictable and the unexpected is most peoples favorite place to be.  And hopefully, as the unexpected becomes a part of your listening repertoire you can move on to more complex music.

comments.name: Becky
comments.body: One of my favorites as well, and I'm a grown woman!  I love the Maui character in particular, and Moana's rapport with him.  When I bought my nephew a Maui doll, I wanted to keep it!  So adorable.

comments.name: Thomas Moore
comments.body:
It's the eyes. Who can resist them? 
Meanwhile, I have gone back to the complete soundtrack of the original "Wizard of Oz" along with other musicals and songs from my parent's days. Things I didn't listen to at all during my life until I hit 72.

comments.name: Fg
comments.body: I've watched Moana, Frozen and Encanto with my Grandaughter and absolutely love the music, the characters and the stories. t  I think that it is as simple as  that with no complicated psychological theories needed.

comments.name: Sara
comments.body: For all of the L-M Miranda and/or Disney geeks out there, I can't recommend highly enough my pal Rico Gagliano's interview https://www.dinnerpartydownload.org/lin-manuel-miranda/index.html in order to understand the structure of a Disney movie and the importance of the "I want" song. It's really interesting and inspired me to have 8th grade students compare the "I want" songs in a variety of Disney movies and then create their own character and write her/his "I want" song. Good stuff. Moana's is absolutely the best.

comments.name: AS
comments.body: I wonder if there’s something deeper going on.  Maybe, Moana came on the scene at just the right moment.  Like the Beatles, if the film was released five years earlier or ten years later, would it be as successful?  Does anyone remember hula hoops?  Does anyone remember Davy Crockett?

articles.title: Kids Can’t Stop Watching ‘Moana.’ There’s a Scientific Explanation.
articles.summary: The 2016 release has become the most watched movie on Disney+. Parents and experts explain why kids can’t get enough.

comments.name: Robert
comments.body:
Getting private equity out of buying out pre-existing homes is a win, but that seems to be all there is.

Not sure I really care that much for an acceleration of rental homes. I personally think it's a mirage of home ownership and security with a significantly higher cost than an apartment. Most of the lease rates I've seen would require the landlords to be more "flexible" with income requirements and leave the renters in a position where they're paying the equivalent to a mortgage that they wouldn't have been able to qualify for.

Unfortunately without the ability for a federal level housing authority to overrule zoning restrictions, this is going to fall flat in the long run. Without changing our country's views on housing being an investment that should match or beat the S&P 500's, returns rather than a place to live that retains value equal to maintenance/renovation, we'll never see the political will to enact serious change.

comments.name: Tony Frank
comments.body: The markets will eventually find the solution as government interference is seldom the better choice except for what it does for the well-to-do.

comments.name: Jack Smythe
comments.body: Affordable housing is an issue in practically all the western economic countries, and has been for decades. It is one of the unsolved issues that has helped bring into power, or make viable,  the authoritarian political parties that have, or are likely to, take over what were formerly democracies. Not that they will do any better.

comments.name: E
comments.body: I think people upset about the build to rent phenomenon are likely confusing cause and effect. Prices aren't high because investors are buying up rentals. Investors have been buying up rentals because not enough individuals can save up the down payment, which is usually 15-20% of the price post GFC. People still need to live somewhere and those who do have the cash for the down payment will be the ones buying. The only way to really help young people save down payments faster is to encourage wage growth, lower college costs, and overall allow savings rates to increase. The top 20% or so maybe getting down payment assistance from their parents but doing something like this on a national scale would cost a lot. A tax break for builders to produce starter homes would also help because margins on those are low. In many states new homes now cost less than used comparable homes but both cost more monthly than renting - by a lot. House prices aren't consistent with today's level of mortgage rates, that's the basic problem.

comments.name: Jean
comments.body:
Look up “ The Cube House” in Rotterdam, Netherlands.

Wonderful, innovative multi unit housing.  Charming addition to neighborhood.

comments.name: Jean
comments.body:
Starter homes aren’t the only need.

Many seniors want to remain on own, but downsize — and on one level ( no stairs).
If there was more new such condo or apartment buildings for the seniors ( and mixed ages), it would open up the 2,500+ square foot multi bedroom homes so many seniors are ready to leave.

And include underground, or attached garages!!  ( who wants to age with risk of falls in bad weather walking to and from car outside?)

comments.name: Sam
comments.body: I’m in disbelief how low American’s are willing to settle in such a short period of time. This bill appears to me as a framework to bifurcate a lower tier into the housing market. Mobile homes were never attractive “investments” and I highly doubt removing the “permanent chassis” language will make them so now. No one would consider living in a FEMA trailer a step up in life so, I don’t get the fanfare surrounding this bill. It seems Congress is suggesting new house market entrants purchase a mobile home (that’s not mobile) to build equity so that they may enter the luxury (brick and mortar) housing market. I doubt you’d see anyone in Congress in such a “house”. We’ve truly entered the phase of the American Dream where you need to be asleep to believe it.

comments.name: Chris R
comments.body: A $1M "penalty" for exceeding 350 homes is just a blip, the cost of doing business. Meaningless.

articles.title: What’s in the Housing Bill That Just Became Law
articles.summary: It is no Great Society measure, but the new law offers local governments and builders incentives to make incremental changes.

comments.name: Loden
comments.body:
Like so many advice columns, the comments focus not on what the letter says but some other more familiar situation commenters would rather address.

LW dislikes the behavior of a relative who shows up at family gatherings and seeks advice on dealing w/ that relative.

The side story is a cousin purported to struggle w/ addiction.  Many comments accuse LW of negativity regarding addiciton, but LW  expresses no opinions of the cousin or addicts in general and does not ask for advice about dealing w/ the cousin.

Some demand LW get involved in helping the cousin but we know nothing about their relationship.  Wanting to help an addict is a noble but assigning that duty to LW with what little we know is reckless.

But many comments accuse LW of negativity regarding addiction and not getting involved enough.

comments.name: Liz
comments.body: To me it sounds as if you simply do not like your aunt and uncle and you are using your cousin's supposed drug addiction as the excuse to not like them. How about this: just admit you don't want to be around them because you don't like them. If you have real concerns about your cousin then talk to her. Being direct is the kindest thing you can do if your cousin is an addict and allows her to put that idea to rest if she is not.

comments.name: Your Neighbor
comments.body:
Talk to the cousin, offer some help, and tell the aunt.

I've done this a bunch of times. Helped one of them and make a lot of people angry with me and lost friends and professional connections in all the others, but I can sleep at night.

They're in pain, and they need help.  Do you walk past someone lying on the ground with a broken leg?

comments.name: Henry
comments.body: The writer doesn’t say what course of action she’s being prevented from taking. What would their interaction with their family member be if she weren’t maintaining kayfabe? Is she asking for permission to initiate an intervention? Have a “serious conversation” with the aunt and uncle? Openly bad mouth about the cousin in front of family? The question of whether it is OK for the writer to do or say what they’d really like to entirely depends on what exactly it is they are planning on doing or saying!

comments.name: SD
comments.body: Despite what the advice giver says, this is not your business.

comments.name: JET
comments.body: I’m unclear as to what evidence the letter writer has that their cousin has been struggling with drug addiction since this information must originally have come to them second- or third-hand from several states away. Now the only evidence is the cousin’s appearance and demeanor. How do they know that the aunt is not telling the truth, that the daughter has trouble sleeping. I have a friend who suffers from severe sleep deprivation due to medically resistant restless legs syndrome (RLS) who presents in exactly the same way – like a zombie, hunched over with hollowed eyes. I bet people who don’t know her also think she is a drug addict.

comments.name: Karen K.
comments.body: This person doesn't like her aunt very much and it's likely the feeling is mutual.  Why would the aunt discuss a deeply persona issue with this particular family member?  It's none of her business.  If letter writer has a relationship with and cares about her cousin she can try talking to her directly.

comments.name: Mist
comments.body:
Try talking to the uncle. If “he meekly acquiesces” he may actually have a different opinion of the situation, but does not want the argument with his wife.  Then, as long as it goes well the uncle, try talking directly to the cousin.

As far as all the comments calling LW selfish for worrying how to handle the situation, stop.  They wrote in to find a way for them to deal with the aunt, not how to get his cousin off drugs.  Being fed up with the aunt’s refusal to either admit or even just see reality, and tired of her outlandish lies, they feel they can’t play along anymore.  They do not see the cousin frequently,  they are not ‘best friends’.  As stated here, you can’t make an addict give it up.  They have to want to.

articles.title: My Aunt Pretends My Cousin Doesn’t Have a Drug Problem. Do I Have to Play Along?
articles.summary: I am sick of the charade we are expected to maintain around them.

articles.title: How to Invest When the Global Crises Never Stop
articles.summary: In a world of wars, trade wars and crop failures, bond yields need to be higher than they were because they offer so much less protection than they used to.

comments.name: Lewis Howard
comments.body: Invest primarily in index funds, short term bonds and cash for the long haul, then buy things like BMNR and EVC from time to time to make a quick buck and invest the proceeds long term.  Safe and fun.

comments.name: Cecil Patterson
comments.body: I can't imagine anything worse than COVID.  Businesses were shutting down, people were dying yet within 18 months the market was setting new highs.

comments.name: Rick C
comments.body: Can Macintosh point to any recent or ongoing crop failures?

comments.name: Gino Marchetti
comments.body: If you want to invest in bonds but are worried about inflation then it makes sense to buy Tips.  VTIP and SCHP are good choices to add to your portfolio (Just pick your duration risk).

comments.name: Raghu K
comments.body: Follow the rich? They seem to be increasing their wealth no matter what.

comments.name: Bill Cottrell
comments.body: The world has always been in turmoil as long as people inhabit the earth, it will continue. Global Warming?. That statement removed all doubt, this writer has no credibility. Invest consistently, for the long term. Don't get consumed by noise like this article.

comments.name: DOUGLAS HAGER
comments.body:
"Because we need higher returns to make up for the risks."

Interesting take from Mr. Arndt. I would flip what he said. "We need to take more risk, because we need higher returns." And I wouldn't agree with that either.

comments.name: G Sanfur
comments.body:
Not a day goes by, I do not get an ad on my computer or something in my mailbox telling someone has something I need for my investment portfolio.  As an old retired guy, I have read and listened to a lot of it.   

No one knows what the market will do.  There will be thousands of predictions and a few will turn out to be true, but it's only by luck.  If anyone could predict the market, we'd all be very rich.

My 50/50 portfolio, spread across all sectors with my buy and hold strategy has held up.  There are people that imply they know some kind of investing secret to beat the system.  Run from these people.  About half the time they are selling annuities. 

I have talked to FA's, done a lot of individual research and now leverage AI on my investment strategy.  Nothing has made me want to change my buy and hold strategy.  Living off dividends while the portfolio continues to grow works for me.  It's worked for years. 

I think a lot of people "play" the market trying to time winners and losers because they did not save enough over the long haul and benefited from compounding.

articles.summary: For the third straight game, the defending champions suffered through a nail-biter. And for a third straight game, Lionel Messi and Co. prevailed.

comments.name: B Ginsburg
comments.body:
A very unimpressive series of games by the Argentines, their success has been mostly a result of good fortune coupled with poor decisions by their opponents.

Unlikely to happen in the semi.

comments.name: David Benson
comments.body: I have no problem with what happened to Embolo. I detest diving. But it's the unequal application of the rules that irks me. Early in the first half Messi took a dive just outside the penalty box. He got the ball, dribbled for a bit to maneuver to his favorite spot just outside the semicircle at the top of the box, lost the ball, and then dove to the ground like he'd been shot. Watch a replay. comments.name: Charles Stephenson

comments.name: Carlos Diaz

There’s nothing to be gained by agreeing with or disabusing any of these nice folks; small money, no political value.  Other cults and religions, though, are useful, and have decent payoffs.  Faith has nothing to do with reason.  If anything it appeals most to those who find reason and reality painful.

Almost.

comments.name: Stephen Johnson

comments.name: Keith Dowling

comments.name: Susan Timko

comments.name: Thomas Cooper
comments.body: When I hear the phrase "dollar cost averaging", I know I can stop reading.

comments.name: Alice
comments.body: Here in Delmarva we have delicious fried chicken as well as the legendary eastern shore style rotisserie chicken grilling along roadsides. And scrapple! Our beaches are beautiful, diverse and well maintained. There is a RoFo (Royal Farms) within walking distance to my favorite beach. So no thanks to the garish displays of money in the Hamptons.

comments.name: JJ
comments.body:
Always interesting to see so many young people in expensive places like the Hamptons, expensive restaurants in NYC etc.

Flying across the pond, walking to my economy seat,  it is striking to see that most of the people in business class are under 45.

comments.name: Louden Swain
comments.body: Not one, as in, zero, of these people eating Popeye’s at Surf Lodge will ever set foot into an actual Popeyes restaurant, now or after Labor Day. This is simply a brand wanting to sit on the cool side of the cafeteria. Certainly, they paid for their cafeteria seat but will soon be forgotten when the crowds return to the City. comments.name: Brad
comments.body:
“She called it The McNuggetini. The group loved it, she said.

“It was literally like eating at McDonald’s,” Ms. Blutstein said. “It was so savory.”

“Her nugget cocktail is not currently on any menus, though she plans to serve it at an industry party in September, a possible next step toward a public-facing version of the McNuggetini.”

comments.name: sandra M
comments.body: If you click the link for the commercial designer, she has a lot of fun videos.  One was telling the difference on how you order food between LA and NY and had all the stereotypes that LA has garnered over the years including the healthy and organic tropes.  I'm from the LA area and would never think of having chicken fingers/tenders.  I guess she's right lol.

comments.name: Bob
comments.body:
It's astonishing how little self confidence seemingly successful people have to be conned into such ridiculousness. Just because you can afford such nonsense doesn't mean you should actually do it.  Common sense just isn't so common... 

And yes I live out East and can well afford to do it but choose not too.  But hey, you do you.

comments.name: jeff
comments.body:
Interesting to read how folks with too much money live.  

Personally I've found cheap rotisserie chicken and a cold bottle of white white, maybe some chopped melon and berries, or a baguette and cheese works.   Throw down a blanket and feast with friends.  

No caviar needed, and I do like caviar.  Bit fancy for the beach though.

My all time favorite beach meal was when a bunch of us just out of high school flipped rocks on a remote Maine shore, gathered driftwood, seaweed and lobsters, rolling the lobsters in the seasweed and roasting them among the buried driftwood coals.  

We might have had some cheap beer and a watermelon or two, but those seaweed wrapped lobsters, freely gathered, cooked with nothing but what was at hand, were better than any fancy restaurant meal I've had.  

I've had some good luck dining too, over the years, on 5 continents, and I've enjoyed spicy street foods as well as rooftop villas with waiting lists. 

Still, a thrown together picnic with friends always beats the fanciest spread at a corporate get away.  People matter, the environment matters, being genuine and in the moment matters.  

The food?  Bring a rotisserie chicken and some cold drinks.  Or slice open a melon on the spot or, God forbid, stop for chicken fingers if you must.  

Just enjoy being together outside. Or alone, for that matter.  

My second best meal was some grapes pulled off a vine in Venice and eaten on a harbor bench by myself, at dawn, while the tourists slept.

comments.name: Matthew
comments.body: In my college days we would go to Summers on the Beach and soak up the rays, drink cold ones and down the hot dogs and burgers Summers offered on their menus and they were wonderful. It is a shame the current generation will never know the Hamptons of the early 1980’s. Great memories!

articles.title: In the Hamptons, Even the Chicken Tenders Are Living Fancy
articles.summary: It’s summer on the South Fork. Care for some nuggets and caviar?

comments.name: Garfield
comments.body:
"To ensure that you can benefit from this provision, you’ll need to collect as much evidence as possible to bolster the case that your city apartment is your principal residence"

"Bolster the case"?  What case?  There is no case unless the IRS orders an audit.  There are millions of home sales a year and the chances of becoming involved in a "case" seem remote.  Collection of tax records is essential for tax filing purposes, but the assertion that a home sale means that the seller will likely become involved in an IRS "case" is absurd.

comments.name: EJ
comments.body:
Before the May1997 tax law change, I believe there was no exclusion on capital gains tax when selling a primary home. Taxes were owed on the full net profit.  

The advantage of the pre-1997 tax law over the current one is that capital gains tax could be avoided entirely if the proceeds from a primary home sale were rolled over into an equally or more expensive primary home within 24 months.

comments.name: CHL
comments.body: My husband has health issues that, while not immediately terminal, leave us to believe he will predecease me. Someone suggested we transfer our home ownership from joint to him alone and modify his will to leave me the house. I would supposedly gain all the "stepped-up basis" benefits, and avoid capital gains tax altogether.

comments.name: Heiko Roloff
comments.body:
There are no capital gains tax in Germany nor in Costa Rica when you sell your primary home. Nor in any other country I know except for the land of the FREE. Hmm. And btw: The real estate in both countries mentioned is minimal. A fee hundred dollar a year. Not 20K or more for a million Dollar home.
Maybe this is way gen Z rather buys stocks than hom. And maybe if America fixes that, a home is an investment or nest again. I mean, America is after all the land of OWNERSHIP, no?
#

comments.name: EJ
comments.body:
The current capital gains tax exclusion limits were established in 1997.  In 1997, the median U.S. home price was approximately $127,000. Nowadays, that amount reflects the cost of a car. 

Because inflation has significantly pushed up today’s home values, a massive chunk of the "gain" on a home sale is just keeping pace with inflation; it is not actual profit. This results in a significant tax burden to homeowners upon a home sale, even though their purchasing power hasn't changed.  The taxes owed upon a home sale would consume a significant portion of the equity needed for a new home.  This is why many older adults stay in the homes they’ve owned for decades, even though they would prefer to downsize.

comments.name: Tim Olsen
comments.body:
Paying NYC income tax helps a lot as well.

Also, note that depending on carrier, tax authorities can get your location via your phone's GPS without a warrant.  This can be helpful if you are actually physically present in NYC 184 days out of the year.  There are also apps available that will track you and email you a daily PDF showing you where you were.  That can help as well, especially if you don't want to have to rely on the tax authority to request your GPS records from your carrier.

Also, be sure to register to vote in NYC!  Get your driver's license address changed, etc...

comments.name: David
comments.body: Maybe you should be willing to pay your taxes.   People with 2 or 3 homes should pay more.

comments.name: fred herriman
comments.body: And be sure you comply with IRS Pub 523, as others have already pointed out.  See https://www.irs.gov/publications/p523.

comments.name: Carol Robins
comments.body: At work, special ash trays were provided for the smokers. Soon after that, they were asked to go into a separate room. I grew up around smoking parents and couldn't tolerate smoke. Now we have to worry about third-hand smoke, the residual from a hotel room where someone has smoked and and where someone's clothes have retained the substances.

comments.name: Robert Shaffer
comments.body: I started smoking in the Army in the late 1960s. They gave us cigarettes in our rations, and when the sergeant said, "the lamp was lit," we could take a smoke break. I quit smoking in 1987. Two years ago, after having a CT scan for another issue in my heart, it showed a 7mm nodule in my lung. The medical people said not to worry unless it gets larger. But every six months I get another CT scan. So far so good. The question I can't get answered is: what is it? The doctors say, don't worry. If it gets larger, then there are options. I think I do worry. I wonder, does the Army still issue ration packs with cigarettes in them?  Probably not.

comments.name: MF
comments.body:
Growing up in the 60s and 70s, my mother smoked 2-3 packs of Pall Mall every day. My grandmother smoked at least a pack of Marlbooro's or Raleigh every day, and my oldest brother smoked Kools. There were always ashtrays filled up everywhere, and the house smelled of smoke. I didn't know that wasn't normal, you got used to it.  All those family members died of lung cancer. My father, who didn't live with us, also died of lung cancer. My childhood cat died of lung cancer. 

A nodule was discovered on my lung during a CT scan for something else. The doctor didn't seem worried because it was small and I have never smoked. Should I worry?

comments.name: Murhatroid
comments.body: I smoked two packs (or more) a day for decades and stopped 20 years ago. My wonderful GP, a pulmonologist, advised me to lie about my quit date so I could continue getting annual lung screenings. Lung cancer often comes for ex-smokers many, many years after we quit. The scans are so important.

comments.name: Me
comments.body: I routinely read the obituaries. This morning I saw a woman's obit  I had not thought of in years, but there she was dead at 86 of recently diagnosed lung cancer.  I remembered her from book club 40 years ago. She was a brilliant, acerbic,  chain-smoking, hacking lady. My first thought was shock that she lasted that long.

comments.name: mhnicholas
comments.body: A few years ago, I wanted my 64-year-old husband to get this lung cancer screening. However, he did not meet any of the criteria. He was a light smoker, 5 to 10 cigarettes a day, and he had quit more than 15 years ago. Well guess what, in mid-February of this year, he was diagnosed with stage 4 lung cancer with brain mets. And he has two of the most aggressive mutations that have no FDA approved oral targeted therapy. For years, we've heard the message that no matter how little you smoke, you can get lung cancer, and yet the criteria prevent anyone who has smoked from getting this screening. I guess we could have paid for it out of pocket, so that was a failure of imagination on our part, thinking that the reasoning for the criteria was because people who don't meet the criteria are probably at a lower risk for lung cancer. I don't know why we didn't think about it or pushed our doctor on this matter. But the criteria should be changed so that at least, anyone who has smoked long term can get the screening. For those who get lung cancer and have never smoked, I don't know what the answer is for that population. The problem I've discovered with lung cancer is that often the diagnosis comes in the late stages of the disease. No symptoms. By the time my husband was diagnosed, he had 20+leasions in his brain. He did not have a seizure, but having a seizure sometimes leads to a lung cancer diagnosis.  He had some neurological problems with balance and the left side of his body.

comments.name: Viju
comments.body: My mom a non smoker in a non smoking household was diagnosed with lung cancer when the radiologist noticed a spot on her CT scan for a different unrelated cancer that she was being monitored for post surgery. They rushed her to surgery and took out 3 lobes of her lung. She’s lucky it was caught early as she had no smoking history. Her other cancer of the jaw is common in tobacco chewers and she had never done that either but had to have her jaw replaced. Two cancers in one person with one of the risk factors for those. Scans save lives and should be provided to non smokers exposed to smoke including heavy pollution.

comments.name: D
comments.body: Truly hope the pack-year calculation is eliminated and replaced with coverage for scans on a recurrence interval similar to colonoscopies tor those with more than minimal smoking history or other recurring smoke exposure/risk factors.  It’s frustrating to have this early detection tool out of reach for those of us who have asked for it but dont qualify under the pack year calculation. Thanks to the person who mentioned upper back pain as tied to a lung nodule. I’ll be following up with my doc.

These fictional and the real life paramedics are certainly an example for me, for nobody can question their toughness, coolness under pressure and danger, dedication to their difficult work, and the care and compassion they have. Can't run on hard surfaces anymore. The buoyancy of the sea greatly reduces the pounding your joints take when compared to running on land. Here is a description of my water running/jogging I have posted before in the NY Times from several years ago: 

So wish I could share a video and/or a photo of my water "gym" here in Greece...former marathon runner here with two replaced hips, who had to stop running, and man!, I was addicted to the runner's high I used to get. Now, at age 61, I get it again, by water jogging in the most amazingly crystal clear and calm water at my local uncrowded beach here on a Greek island. I run, forwards and backwards, at a pretty good clip, in the sea up to my chest. Arms are submerged as well, my bare feet on soft firm sand...I will take several dives during my one hour run in the sea, to cool off even more. Today it is almost 100 degrees here. comments.body: It used to be that a fictional character committing amoral acts would be called an antihero, and that the narrative would punish them with comeuppance or at least a bittersweet ending. We may sympathize, but it would be a complex form of identification, and the book would provide catharsis insofar as we've experienced and worked through discomfort, that most important human emotion for the process of learning and growth. To be (reductively) clinical about it, this has always been the basic social function of taboo in fiction. Perhaps that's the case in many of these books. But I kept waiting for this article to mention how these narratives treat their complex heroes, whether there's any sense that they're actually the bad guys, and that it did not come, I end up feeling more discomfited than I have by many taboo novels. I am experiencing female rage at the idea that abject and extreme violence is now treated as a garden variety metaphor. But then, I always find "shock value" tedious. Reaching straight for extremes often belies an inability on the writer's part to explore subtlety.

comments.name: 0islessthan1
comments.body:
A candidate reason for a flurry of novels involving cannibalism (or any other topic integral to a recent bestseller) is the herd mentality of profit-seeking writers. One novel involving cannibalism does well and one hundred profit-seeking novelists lacking the ability or courage for original thought say, "I can do that."

I'm not knocking profit-seeking. Writers gotta eat too. Yet the copycat mentality is problematic within the arts, particularly in the arts of storytelling, such as books and movies.

However, since it is far easier to create a presentable book (typically requiring far fewer people and a significantly smaller budget) than a presentable movie, the problem is even greater in the publishing industry than im the film industry.

Much as filmgoers lament the prevalence of sequels and pine for filmmakers to create something (seemingly) new (perhaps with a contemporary spin), discerning readers wish for writers to conjure something (again, seemingly) new.

The bar is even higher for books than movies, as readers have orders of magnitude more great works produced across several centuries to choose from.

Writers who derive their primary income from writing (and their publishers) are in a bind and lack the luxury of taking risk to create something truly new. Fortunately for these symbiotic players, marketing departments are immense, literary education and awareness are in decline, and there is a sucker born every minute.

"Stories of people-eating have captivated audiences for centuries, even millenniums[...]" There is nothing that makes me want to take a fresh bite out of someone's throat like seeing the word "millenniums" in print, rather than the much more pleasing "millennia." But this, too, shall eventually pass, along with the capers in my liver pudding. Anyway, I'm off to the buffet bar now. I've filled up on finger food and am jonesing for a hand sandwich.

This is a question for anyone who isn’t Norwegian or English: Who will you be cheering for in tonight’s quarterfinal? 

Norway has emerged as the feel-good team of the tournament. The Viking Row is infectious, and it seems everyone wants to be Erling Haaland’s friend. It’s not hard to see why so many people, even some English fans, are backing them tonight. 

On the other hand, the pressure is on for England and some fans I spoke to would not even dare to hope. And yet, they do. Every generation of England’s national team hopes to be the one to bring the cup home to the birthplace of football (aka soccer). The frown on Harry Kane’s face says it all.

comments.body: It was interesting to see how much public art Yaacov Agam made. I had never seen it before! Those fountains, but also building facades. And semi-public work like a piece he made to commemorate the 1979 peace treaty between Egypt and Israel. From one side it resembles the star of David, from another the star of Islam. He worked often with Gobelins, the historic tapestry workshop in France. One of his multicolored rugs, which took three years to weave and is composed of 180 shades, is still in the Elysée Palace, and shows up in photos of President Emmanuel Macron in interviews, or entertaining heads of state. President Macron, in a statement issued at his death, called Agam “an artist of France and a son of Israel.”
